title: The hangover of oppression: An ecological momentary assessment study of oppression-based stressors and daily alcohol use and hazardous drinking outcomes among sexual and gender minoritized young adults.
abstract: Sexual and gender minoritized (SGM) young adults are at greater risk for hazardous drinking and alcohol use disorder (AUD) than their heterosexual and cisgender counterparts. These inequities are often explained with oppression frameworks, which posit that oppression-based stressors (i.e., discrimination) contribute to hazardous drinking and the development of AUD. However, research examining the daily and within-person associations between oppression-based stressors and alcohol use among SGM young adults is nascent and equivocal. We conducted a 30-day ecological momentary assessment of daily within- and between-person oppression-based stressors and same-day alcohol use outcomes (i.e., alcohol use, quantity of drinks, heavy drinking, alcohol-related consequences, hangover symptoms) among 98 SGM young adults who engaged in heavy drinking (71.4% met criteria for AUD). We also examined multiple person-level moderators (e.g., sociodemographics, addiction severity, stress exposure and sensitivity) to identify for whom oppression-based stressors confer risk for hazardous drinking. Results indicated that on days participants experienced more oppression-based stressors than their average, they reported greater odds of daily heavy drinking. Participants who experienced greater oppression-based stressors overall reported more daily negative and positive alcohol-related consequences and hangovers. The within-person associations between oppression-based stressors and some of the hazardous drinking outcomes were moderated by AUD symptoms, a family history of alcohol problems, greater lifetime exposure to cisheterosexism, and identification as plurisexual (e.g., bisexual). Our findings provide support for oppression and addiction frameworks and further highlight risks that plurisexual young adults experience. The results underscore the need to target oppression to reduce hazardous drinking among SGM young adults. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).
